claim: Information that is shared across brains is encoded in idiosyncratic fine-scale functional topographies.
source: Information that is shared across brains is encoded in idiosyncratic fine-scale functional topographies.
evidence: This is a central thesis statement of the manuscript that is supported by multiple experimental results and computational models presented throughout the paper.

claim: Hyperalignment captures shared information by projecting pattern vectors for neural responses and connectivities into a common, high-dimensional information space.
source: Hyperalignment captures shared information by projecting pattern vectors for neural responses and connectivities into a common, high-dimensional information space, rather than by aligning topographies in a canonical anatomical space.
evidence: This describes the core computational approach of hyperalignment, which is demonstrated through multiple implementations and validation tests.

claim: Individual transformation matrices preserve the geometry of pairwise dissimilarities between pattern vectors.
source: Individual transformation matrices project information from individual anatomical spaces into the common model information space, preserving the geometry of pairwise dissimilarities between pattern vectors
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the Procrustes transformation used in hyperalignment, validated through experimental results.

claim: The fundamental property of brain function that is preserved across brains is information content, rather than the functional properties of local features that support that content.
source: The fundamental property of brain function that is preserved across brains is information content, rather than the functional properties of local features that support that content.
evidence: This is a key conceptual claim supported by the observation that hyperalignment can align information while remixing functional profiles.

claim: Multivariate pattern analysis of fMRI data revealed that information can be decoded from fine-grained patterns of cortical activity.
source: The introduction of multivariate pattern analysis of fMRI data (MVPA; Haxby, 2012; Haxby et al., 2014; Haxby et al., 2011; Haxby et al., 2001) revealed that information can be decoded from fine-grained patterns of cortical activity (see also Bzdok, 2017; Haynes, 2015; Haynes and Rees, 2006; Hebart and Baker, 2018; Norman et al., 2006; Pereira et al., 2009; Tong and Pratte, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Study of cortical functional connectivity has revealed fine-grained topographies in the connectome.
source: Study of cortical functional connectivity also has revealed fine-grained topographies in the connectome (Arcaro et al., 2015; Haak et al., 2018; Heinzle et al., 2011; Jbabdi et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on functional connectivity.

claim: Fine-grained topographies in the connectome are closely related to patterns of activity.
source: Study of cortical functional connectivity also has revealed fine-grained topographies in the connectome (Arcaro et al., 2015; Haak et al., 2018; Heinzle et al., 2011; Jbabdi et al., 2013) that are closely related to these patterns of activity (Guntupalli et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guntupalli et al., 2018.

claim: The surface structure of functional cortical topographies shows considerable variability across individual brains for encoding the same information.
source: The surface structure of functional cortical topographies, however, shows considerable variability across individual brains for encoding the same information (Cox and Savoy, 2003; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research demonstrating inter-individual variability.

claim: Hyperalignment derives from the term hyperspace to convey the paradigm shift from modeling cortical functional architecture in a three-dimensional anatomical space to modeling the information encoded in functional architecture in a high-dimensional information space.
source: Hyperalignment derives from the term hyperspace, to convey the paradigm shift from modeling cortical functional architecture in a three-dimensional anatomical space to modeling the information encoded in functional architecture in a high-dimensional information space.
evidence: This explains the etymology and conceptual motivation for the term 'hyperalignment'.

claim: The common information space captures the 'deep structure' of shared information that is encoded in the variable 'surface structure' of idiosyncratic topographies in individual brains.
source: This common information space captures the 'deep structure' of shared information that is encoded in the variable 'surface structure' of idiosyncratic topographies in individual brains.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim about the nature of the common model space, supported by the overall framework and results.

claim: Information is contained in the relationships among pattern vectors – distinctions and similarities.
source: Information is contained in the relationships among pattern vectors – distinctions and similarities – and these relationships are preserved when the space is transformed from an individual cortical space to the common information space.
evidence: This defines how information is operationalized in the hyperalignment framework.

claim: In hyperalignment transformations, the features that define the space in individual brains are remixed to support the same information structure with shared basis functions.
source: In these transformations, the features that define the space in individual brains – response tuning functions and connectivity profiles – are remixed to support the same information structure with shared basis functions.
evidence: This describes a key property of the transformation matrices derived through hyperalignment.

claim: Shared information is decomposed into overlapping basis functions that are instantiated in individual brains with idiosyncratic topographies.
source: Shared information is decomposed into overlapping basis functions that are instantiated in individual brains with idiosyncratic topographies.
evidence: This describes the computational model of cortical functional architecture proposed by hyperalignment.

claim: Cortical patterns of activity and connectivity are modeled as mixtures of topographic basis functions.
source: Cortical patterns of activity and connectivity are modeled as mixtures of these topographic basis functions.
evidence: This describes how individual cortical patterns are represented in the hyperalignment framework.

claim: The topographic information embedded in the model's shared bases is not strongly constrained by areal boundaries.
source: Our common model accounts for coarse areal structure insofar as the model's shared basis set for fine-scale topographies can be mixed to identify the boundaries for functional areas in individual brains, but the topographic information embedded in the model's shared bases is not strongly constrained by these areal boundaries
evidence: This is supported by analyses showing that areal boundaries account for only a small portion of variance in the model.

claim: Areal structure may play a smaller role in how information is organized in cortex than was previously believed.
source: the topographic information embedded in the model's shared bases is not strongly constrained by these areal boundaries, suggesting that areal structure may play a smaller role in how information is organized in cortex than was previously believed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that areal boundaries do not strongly constrain the model's basis functions.

claim: For fMRI data, local pattern elements are typically voxels or vertices on the cortical surface.
source: For fMRI data, local pattern elements are typically voxels (or vertices on the cortical surface).
evidence: This is a standard description of fMRI data structure.

claim: The relevance of the hyperalignment conceptual framework for modeling cortical functional architecture is not specific to any measurement modality or neural variable.
source: The relevance of the hyperalignment conceptual framework for modeling cortical functional architecture is not specific to any measurement modality or neural variable
evidence: This is supported by examples of applying hyperalignment to different modalities and even artificial neural networks.

claim: The computational procedures of hyperalignment can be applied to data matrices obtained with other measurement modalities.
source: the computational procedures can also be applied to data matrices obtained with other measurement modalities (e.g. Chen et al., 2020) or even artificial neural networks (Lu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to work applying hyperalignment to other data types.

claim: The row vectors in data matrices serve as indices of the brain state corresponding to a given stimulus or cognitive state.
source: The row vectors may be patterns of activity at different points in time or response patterns recovered from multiple instances of a given event or experimental manipulation (using trial averaging or deconvolution) and serve as indices of the brain state corresponding to a given stimulus or cognitive state.
evidence: This describes how row vectors in the data matrix are interpreted.

claim: Information is defined as relationships among functional pattern vectors, typically quantified as the similarity or dissimilarity between each pair of vectors.
source: Here, we define 'information' as relationships among functional pattern vectors, typically quantified as the similarity (or dissimilarity/distance) between each pair of vectors (Connolly et al., 2012; Connolly et al., 2011; Edelman et al., 1998; Hanson et al., 2004; Kriegeskorte et al., 2008a; Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013; O'Toole et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a formal definition supported by citations to prior work using this framework.

claim: Vectors that are more similar to each other are located nearer to each other in vector space.
source: These dissimilarities index the distinctiveness of each vector relative to other vectors; vectors that are more similar to each other are located nearer to each other in vector space.
evidence: This is a basic property of vector space geometry.

claim: The geometric framework for operationalizing information as the relationships among distributed patterns in a vector space is used in a variety of fields.
source: This geometric framework for operationalizing information as the relationships among distributed patterns in a vector space is used in a variety of fields, including psychology (e.g. Edelman, 1998; Shepard, 1987), information retrieval (e.g. Salton et al., 1975), and natural language processing (e.g. Deerwester et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to work in multiple fields.

claim: The vector geometry of information in cortical spaces is highly similar across brains.
source: The vector geometry of information in cortical spaces is highly similar across brains (Connolly et al., 2016; Connolly et al., 2012; Connolly et al., 2011; Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte, 2017; Guntupalli et al., 2018; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013; Nastase et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Hyperalignment leverages the inter-individual similarity of vector geometry to create a shared information space that minimizes differences between corresponding vectors across individuals while preserving vector geometry.
source: Hyperalignment leverages the inter-individual similarity of vector geometry to create a shared information space that minimizes differences between corresponding vectors across individuals while preserving vector geometry.
evidence: This describes the computational strategy of hyperalignment.

claim: The columns of data matrices in the common model space are the coordinate axes or dimensions for that information space.
source: The columns of data matrices in the common model space are the coordinate axes or dimensions for that information space.
evidence: This describes the structure of the common model space data matrix.

claim: The dimensions in the common model space are weighted sums of nearby anatomical locations in individual brains.
source: The dimensions in the common model space are no longer anatomical locations but, rather, are weighted sums of nearby anatomical locations in individual brains
evidence: This describes how model dimensions relate to anatomical locations.

claim: The transformations are not a one-to-one mapping from cortical loci to common space dimensions.
source: the transformations are not a one-to-one mapping from cortical loci to common space dimensions.
evidence: This is a property of the transformation matrices.

claim: The distribution of transformation weights is specific to each brain.
source: The distribution of these weights is specific to each brain.
evidence: This describes the individual-specific nature of transformation matrices.

claim: The number of dimensions in the common space can differ from the number of cortical loci in the data matrices from which the space is derived.
source: The number of dimensions in the common space (m in Figure 2) can differ from the number of cortical loci in the data matrices (k in Figure 2) from which the space is derived.
evidence: This describes a property of the common model space implementation.

claim: In some implementations, the number of model dimensions matches the number of cortical loci in a 'reference brain'.
source: In some implementations, the number of model dimensions matches the number of cortical loci in a 'reference brain', allowing patterns in the model space to be illustrated in the reference brain anatomy (Guntupalli et al., 2018; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes one implementation approach, supported by citations.

claim: In some implementations, the model space is reduced to capture shared information in a smaller number of dimensions and reduce noise or overfitting.
source: In other implementations, the model space is reduced to capture shared information in a smaller number of dimensions and reduce noise or overfitting (Chen et al., 2015; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes another implementation approach, supported by citations.

claim: The coordinate axes for the common information space can be arbitrarily rotated, preserving vector geometry while altering the response tuning and connectivity profiles for the coordinate axes.
source: The coordinate axes for that space – the model dimensions – carry information in the form of shared functional profiles (response tuning vectors or functional connectivity vectors), but they can be arbitrarily rotated, preserving vector geometry while altering the response tuning and connectivity profiles for the coordinate axes.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the vector space representation.

claim: The Procrustes transformation is the orthogonal matrix that minimizes the distances between two matrices of paired vectors with a rigid rotation.
source: The Procrustes transformation is the orthogonal matrix that minimizes the distances between two matrices of paired vectors with a rigid rotation, which is 'improper' in that it allows reflections as well as rotations.
evidence: This is a mathematical definition of the Procrustes transformation.

claim: Generalized Procrustes Analysis finds transformation matrices for a group of data matrices that minimize distances by iteratively aligning each new matrix to the mean of previously aligned matrices.
source: GPA finds transformation matrices for a group of data matrices that minimize distances by iteratively aligning each new matrix to the mean of previously aligned matrices.
evidence: This describes the GPA algorithm.

claim: A rigid rotation preserves all pairwise distances between pattern vectors within each original matrix.
source: A rigid rotation preserves all pairwise distances between pattern vectors within each original matrix.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of rigid rotations.

claim: Local vector geometry is highly correlated across brains.
source: We and others have shown that local vector geometry is highly correlated across brains (Connolly et al., 2016; Connolly et al., 2012; Connolly et al., 2011; Guntupalli et al., 2018; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013; Nastase et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Local vector geometry is a key feature of shared information structure.
source: We and others have shown that local vector geometry is highly correlated across brains (Connolly et al., 2016; Connolly et al., 2012; Connolly et al., 2011; Guntupalli et al., 2018; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013; Nastase et al., 2017), indicating that it is a key feature of shared information structure (Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte, 2017; Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations.

claim: Hyperalignment algorithms that mostly preserve vector geometry tend to generalize better to novel data than algorithms that do not.
source: Hyperalignment algorithms that mostly preserve vector geometry tend to generalize better to novel data than algorithms that do not (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2012.

claim: Whole-cortex searchlight hyperalignment makes local models in overlapping searchlights that cover the cortex, then aggregates the local transformation matrices into a whole-cortex transformation matrix.
source: Whole-cortex searchlight hyperalignment, by contrast, makes local models in overlapping searchlights (Kriegeskorte et al., 2006; Oosterhof et al., 2011) that cover the cortex, then aggregates the local transformation matrices into a whole-cortex transformation matrix, thereby mostly preserving local vector geometry (Guntupalli et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the searchlight hyperalignment algorithm.

claim: Data are aligned anatomically to a standard cortical surface prior to whole-cortex searchlight hyperalignment.
source: Data are aligned anatomically to a standard cortical surface (e.g., FreeSurfer's fsaverage; Fischl et al., 1999) prior to whole-cortex searchlight hyperalignment.
evidence: This describes a preprocessing step in the hyperalignment procedure.

claim: The cortical fields for local basis functions are overlapping and constrained only by searchlight size, not by areal boundaries.
source: The cortical fields for local basis functions, defined by the voxels with nonzero weights in columns of the whole-cortex transformation matrices, are overlapping and constrained only by searchlight size, not by areal boundaries.
evidence: This describes a property of the basis functions derived from searchlight hyperalignment.

claim: A cortical field in the common information space produced by whole-cortex hyperalignment is only defined insofar as it is instantiated in the idiosyncratic cortical topography of an individual brain.
source: A cortical field of contiguous cortical vertices, such as a searchlight or ROI, in the common information space produced by whole-cortex hyperalignment is only defined insofar as it is instantiated in the idiosyncratic cortical topography of an individual brain.
evidence: This describes a conceptual property of cortical fields in the common model space.

claim: Reducing the dimensionality of the common model space using principal component analysis can preserve or even improve performance, as indexed with between-subject multivariate pattern classification.
source: We have shown that reducing the dimensionality of the common model space using principal component analysis (PCA; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011) can preserve or even improve performance, as indexed with between-subject multivariate pattern classification (bsMVPC; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Between-subject MVPC accuracies can be substantially higher with lower dimensional models.
source: Later work suggests that bsMVPC accuracies can be substantially higher with lower dimensional models (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: Dimensionality reduction necessarily warps vector geometry but can effectively denoise data in common space by discarding lower-order eigenvectors.
source: Dimensionality reduction necessarily warps vector geometry but can effectively denoise data in common space by discarding lower-order eigenvectors.
evidence: This describes a trade-off in dimensionality reduction.

claim: With regularized CCA, a small relaxation of the orthogonality constraint enhances performance, as indexed with between-subject multivariate pattern classification.
source: With regularized CCA we find that a small relaxation of the orthogonality constraint enhances performance, as indexed with between-subject multivariate pattern classification (bsMVPC).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' work with rCCA.

claim: The human connectome has fine-grained topographies that are not captured by mean connections between areas.
source: Previous work has shown that the human connectome has fine-grained topographies that are not captured by mean connections between areas (Arcaro et al., 2015; Braga et al., 2019; Haak et al., 2018; Heinzle et al., 2011; Jbabdi et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Connectivity hyperalignment has shown that fine-scale structure in the connectome is prevalent across all of cortex and of higher dimensionality than can be captured with known topographies.
source: connectivity hyperalignment has shown that this fine-scale structure in the connectome is prevalent across all of cortex and of higher dimensionality than can be captured with known topographies, such as retinotopy and orientation selectivity (Guntupalli et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guntupalli et al., 2018.

claim: Connectivity hyperalignment does not require a common stimulus paradigm, affording hyperalignment of resting state data.
source: Whereas response hyperalignment depends on response pattern vectors in experimental data that are locked to stimuli, connectivity hyperalignment depends on connectivity vectors for a defined set of connectivity targets and does not require a common stimulus paradigm, affording hyperalignment of resting state data (Guntupalli et al., 2018) or across different experiments (Nastase et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes an advantage of connectivity hyperalignment, supported by citations.

claim: Transformation matrices derived with connectivity hyperalignment can be applied to response data, effectively aligning response pattern vectors.
source: Transformation matrices derived with connectivity hyperalignment can be applied to response data, effectively aligning response pattern vectors (Guntupalli et al., 2018; Nastase et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Response hyperalignment aligns connectivity information and connectivity hyperalignment aligns population response information.
source: Validation tests show that response hyperalignment aligns connectivity information and connectivity hyperalignment aligns population response information.
evidence: This is supported by validation tests described in the manuscript.

claim: Estimating the parameters to transform high-dimensional spaces from individual brains into a common high-dimensional space requires a rich set of data that samples a wide variety of cortical patterns.
source: Estimating the parameters to transform high-dimensional spaces from individual brains into a common high-dimensional space requires a rich set of data that samples a wide variety of cortical patterns in order to generalize to novel stimuli or tasks.
evidence: This is a requirement for effective hyperalignment, supported by empirical results.

claim: A common model space based on transformation matrices derived from responses to naturalistic audiovisual movies has general validity across a variety of experiments.
source: We have shown that a common model space based on transformation matrices derived from responses to naturalistic audiovisual movies has general validity across a variety of experiments (Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011; Nastase et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Transformation matrices estimated from controlled experiments with a limited set of stimuli or cognitive states do not generalize well to other contexts or paradigms.
source: By contrast, transformation matrices estimated from controlled experiments with a limited set of stimuli or cognitive states may suffice for that experiment, but do not generalize well to other contexts or paradigms (Haxby et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Haxby et al., 2011.

claim: Naturalistic movie stimuli evoke a rich variety of brain states involving multiple coordinated systems.
source: Such stimuli evoke a rich variety of brain states involving multiple coordinated systems for visual and auditory perception, perception of dynamic action, narrative, and speech, memory, attention, semantic knowledge, and social cognition.
evidence: This describes properties of naturalistic movie stimuli.

claim: Movies are engineered to be engaging and guide attention.
source: Movies are engineered to be engaging and guide attention.
evidence: This is a general property of movie stimuli.

claim: Movies build a rich set of expectations for upcoming stimuli and events affording strong predictions.
source: Movies also build a rich set of expectations for upcoming stimuli and events affording strong predictions (and prediction errors).
evidence: This describes a property of movie stimuli relevant to neural processing.

claim: Controlled experiments typically randomize trial order, deliberately decontextualizing each event and providing no basis for accurate prediction.
source: Controlled experiments, on the other hand, typically randomize trial order, deliberately decontextualizing each event and providing no basis for accurate prediction.
evidence: This describes a typical property of controlled experiments.

claim: Between-subject multivariate pattern classification accuracies in ventral temporal extrastriate visual cortex for naturalistic, dynamic stimuli were twice that for unpredictable static stimuli.
source: In a comparison of between-subject multivariate pattern classification (bsMVPC) of responses to dynamic stimuli in movies to bsMVPC of responses to static stimuli in controlled experiments, with the structure of these analyses carefully matched to allow meaningful comparison, bsMVPC accuracies in ventral temporal extrastriate visual cortex for naturalistic, dynamic stimuli were twice that for unpredictable static stimuli (Supplemental Figure 4A in Haxby et al., 2011)
evidence: This is a specific finding from Haxby et al., 2011.

claim: A common model space can be built by estimating transformation matrices from fMRI data collected in the resting state using connectivity hyperalignment.
source: A common model space also can be built by estimating transformation matrices from fMRI data collected in the resting state (rs-fMRI) using connectivity hyperalignment (Guntupalli et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guntupalli et al., 2016.

claim: A common model based on rs-fMRI data greatly increases intersubject correlations of functional connectivity indices and captures the fine-scale spatial structure of variation in connectivity.
source: Such a model greatly increases intersubject correlations of functional connectivity indices and captures the fine-scale spatial structure of variation in connectivity that is seen in individual data.
evidence: This describes the effectiveness of resting-state based hyperalignment.

claim: The general validity of a common model based on rs-fMRI data for aligning brain states associated with a wide variety of stimuli and cognitive processes has not yet been established.
source: The general validity of a common model based on rs-fMRI data for aligning brain states associated with a wide variety of stimuli and cognitive processes has not yet been established.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of current knowledge.

claim: Previous models of cortical functional architecture have focused on the division of cortex into contiguous functional areas.
source: Previous models of cortical functional architecture have focused on the division of cortex into contiguous functional areas (Brodman, 1909; Glasser et al., 2016; Gordon et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2010; Yeo et al., 2011; Zilles and Amunts, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on cortical parcellation.

claim: Cortical parcellations may vary substantially across functional brain state and individuals.
source: These parcellations, however, may vary substantially across functional brain state (Salehi et al., 2020) and individuals (Braga and Buckner, 2017; Gordon et al., 2017; Kong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: The conceptual framework for hyperalignment proposes a radically different basis for cortical topographies that is based on overlapping topographic basis functions.
source: The conceptual framework for hyperalignment proposes a radically different basis for cortical topographies that is based on overlapping topographic basis functions, offering a model that accounts for individual variation in both fine-scale topographies and coarse-scale areal structure.
evidence: This describes the novel contribution of the hyperalignment framework.

claim: Each column in an individual transformation matrix is a pattern vector of weights for cortical loci in an individual subject's brain that serves as a topographic basis function.
source: Each column in an individual transformation matrix (Ri) (or row in the transpose of that matrix, RiT), is a pattern vector of weights for cortical loci in an individual subject's brain. These pattern vectors for model dimensions serve as topographic basis functions.
evidence: This describes how transformation matrices define basis functions.

claim: Patterns that specify an area or topographic pattern in other subjects' cortex can be transformed into a group mean pattern in the common model information space.
source: Patterns that specify an area or topographic pattern, such as a face-responsive area or retinopy, in other subjects' cortex (tp(B)) can be transformed into a group mean pattern in the common model information space (tp(M)) using their transformation matrices
evidence: This describes how group patterns can be derived in the common space.

claim: The mean topographic pattern in the model space can be projected into a new individual's cortical space using that individual's transformation matrix.
source: The mean topographic pattern in the model space (tp(M)) can then be projected into a new individual's cortical space using that individual's transformation matrix and Equation 2, providing an estimate of that pattern (t̂p(Bi)) in that individual's brain.
evidence: This describes how patterns can be transferred to new individuals.

claim: Assessing the performance of hyperalignment requires testing on data that play no role in calculating the parameters in the transformation matrices.
source: Assessing the performance of hyperalignment for modeling shared information and idiosyncratic topographies requires testing on data that play no role in calculating the parameters in the transformation matrices (Kriegeskorte et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a standard principle of cross-validation, supported by citation.

claim: Numerous tests with different data sets have shown marked and robust improvement of intersubject similarity on all indices after hyperalignment.
source: Numerous tests with different data sets have shown marked and robust improvement of intersubject similarity on all of these indices (e.g., Chen et al., 2015; Guntupalli et al., 2018; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011; Nastase et al., 2017; Van Uden et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The magnitude of the beneficial effect of hyperalignment on bsMVPC is largest for small and moderately-sized ROIs which contain fine-scale topographies with minimal coarse-scale variation.
source: The magnitude of the beneficial effect of hyperalignment on bsMVPC is largest for small and moderately-sized ROIs which contain fine-scale topographies with minimal coarse-scale variation, where bsMVPC accuracies for anatomically-aligned data are very low.
evidence: This describes a pattern in the results.

claim: In small cortical regions, hyperalignment provides more than a full order of magnitude improvement in bsMVPC.
source: In small cortical regions, where accuracies for unsmoothed, anatomically aligned data are very low, hyperalignment provides more than a full order of magnitude improvement in bsMVPC (Guntupalli et al., 2018; Guntupalli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a specific finding supported by citations.

claim: Response hyperalignment nearly doubled ISCs of time-series responses to a naturalistic movie.
source: For example, response hyperalignment nearly doubled ISCs of time-series responses to a naturalistic movie (Guntupalli et al., 2016)
evidence: This is a specific finding supported by citation.

claim: ISC increases were even greater for functional connectivity profiles after connectivity hyperalignment.
source: ISC increases were even greater for functional connectivity profiles after connectivity hyperalignment, for both functional connectivities measured during movie viewing and during the resting state (Figure 6; see Guntupalli et al., 2018, for details).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to Figure 6.

claim: Searchlight-based whole-cortex hyperalignment greatly increases ISCs of local representational geometry.
source: Searchlight-based whole-cortex hyperalignment greatly increases ISCs of local representational geometry (Figure 5b; Guntupalli et al., 2018; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Nastase et al., 2017; Van Uden et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 5b.

claim: For naturalistic movies, hyperalignment increased mean ISC of representational geometry across searchlights by 46% to 75%.
source: For naturalistic movies, hyperalignment increased mean ISC of representational geometry across searchlights by 46% to 75% (Guntupalli et al., 2016; Van Uden et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a specific finding supported by citations.

claim: ROI hyperalignment does not change the vector geometry for each individual and has no effect on ISC of vector geometry.
source: Indeed, ROI hyperalignment does not change the vector geometry for each individual and, therefore, has no effect on ISC of vector geometry.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the properties of ROI hyperalignment.

claim: Searchlight hyperalignment resamples information into and out of local cortical fields, thereby increasing the similarity of local information content across subjects.
source: Searchlight hyperalignment, by contrast, resamples information into and out of local cortical fields, thereby increasing the similarity of local information content across subjects.
evidence: This explains the mechanism by which searchlight hyperalignment increases ISC of vector geometry.

claim: The dissimilarity of vector geometry for overlapping cortical fields is substantial.
source: The size of the increase suggests this is a large effect and that the dissimilarity of vector geometry for overlapping cortical fields is substantial.
evidence: This is an inference from the magnitude of ISC increases.

claim: Between-subject MVPC of responses to still images after data were projected into a common space based on responses to a movie was equivalent to or better than within-subject MVPC.
source: For example, bsMVPC of responses to still images of objects, faces, and animals after data were projected into a common space based on responses to a movie was equivalent to or better than within-subject MVPC (Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a specific finding supported by citations.

claim: Higher bsMVPC than within-subject MVPC of hyperaligned data demonstrated the added power of using large multi-subject data sets for training a pattern classifier.
source: Higher bsMVPC than within-subject MVPC of hyperaligned data demonstrated the added power of using large multi-subject data sets for training a pattern classifier, which hyperalignment makes possible.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that bsMVPC can exceed within-subject MVPC.

claim: ISC of representational geometry for responses to brief video clips were greatly increased after data were projected into a common space based on responses to a continuous movie.
source: Similarly, ISC of representational geometry for responses to brief video clips of different categories of animals performing different actions were greatly increased after data were projected into a common space based on responses to a continuous movie (Nastase et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a specific finding supported by citation.

claim: Connectivity hyperalignment makes it possible to derive transformation matrices to project new subjects' cortical space into a model space using connectivity data from experimental paradigms that differ from the experimental paradigm used to derive that common model space.
source: Moreover, connectivity hyperalignment now makes it possible to derive transformation matrices to project new subjects' cortical space into a model space using connectivity data from experimental paradigms (e.g., a movie or the resting state) that differ from the experimental paradigm used to derive that common model space (Guntupalli et al., 2018; Nastase et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Hyperalignment made it possible to create a response pattern template based on other subjects' hyperaligned data for use in new subjects who were never exposed to the stimulus as a target brain state for neurofeedback.
source: In a novel application (Taschereau-Dumouchel et al., 2018), hyperalignment made it possible to create a response pattern template based on other subjects' hyperaligned data for use in new subjects who were never exposed to the stimulus as a target brain state for neurofeedback.
evidence: This is a specific application supported by citation.

claim: Response hyperalignment and connectivity hyperalignment both produce transformation matrices that project data from cortical coordinate spaces into a common model information space.
source: Response and connectivity hyperalignment both produce transformation matrices that project data from cortical coordinate spaces into a common model information space.
evidence: This describes a commonality between the two approaches.

claim: The two algorithms align the vector geometries for related, but distinct types of information – patterns of responses and patterns of connectivity.
source: The two algorithms align the vector geometries for related, but distinct types of information – patterns of responses and patterns of connectivity.
evidence: This describes a difference between the two approaches.

claim: Both response and connectivity hyperalignment algorithms produce transformations that can be used to align either type of data.
source: Both algorithms produce transformations that can be used to align either type of data (Guntupalli et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The common model spaces produced by response and connectivity hyperalignment, while closely related, are not equivalent.
source: but the common model spaces, while closely related, are not equivalent (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Table 1.

claim: Response hyperalignment of movie data increased mean intersubject correlation of connectivity profiles from 0.15 to 0.58, relative to anatomical alignment.
source: Response hyperalignment of movie data increased mean intersubject correlation of connectivity profiles from 0.15 to 0.58, relative to anatomical alignment
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding.

claim: ISC of connectivity profiles are even higher after connectivity hyperalignment (mean ISC = 0.67) than after response hyperalignment.
source: but ISC of connectivity profiles are even higher after connectivity hyperalignment (mean ISC = 0.67).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding.

claim: Connectivity hyperalignment increased mean intersubject correlation of representational geometry from 0.21 to 0.31.
source: Connectivity hyperalignment of the same data increased mean intersubject correlation of representational geometry from 0.21 to 0.31
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding.

claim: Connectivity hyperalignment increased bsMVPC of movie time segments from 1.0% to 10.4%, relative to anatomical alignment.
source: and bsMVPC of movie time segments from 1.0% to 10.4%, relative to anatomical alignment.
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding.

claim: Response hyperalignment produced even higher ISC of representational geometry (mean ISC = 0.32) than connectivity hyperalignment.
source: Response hyperalignment, however, produced even higher ISC of representational geometry (mean ISC = 0.32)
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding.

claim: Response hyperalignment produced higher bsMVPC accuracies (mean = 13.7%) than connectivity hyperalignment.
source: and bsMVPC accuracies (mean = 13.7%).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding.

claim: Individual-specific functional topographies, the locations and borders of category-selective regions in ventral temporal cortex, and the retinotopic topography of early visual cortex can be estimated with high fidelity based on other subjects' topographies with hyperalignment.
source: Individual-specific functional topographies, the locations and borders of category-selective regions in ventral temporal cortex, and the retinotopic topography of early visual cortex can be estimated with high fidelity based on other subjects' topographies with hyperalignment (Figures 7 and 8; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Haxby et al., 2011; Jiahui et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations and references to Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Local correlations in searchlights between estimates based on others subjects' data and estimates based on own data exceeded 0.80 in posterior ventral temporal, lateral occipital, and posterior superior temporal cortices.
source: Local correlations in searchlights between estimates based on others subjects' data and estimates based on own data exceeded 0.80 in posterior ventral temporal, lateral occipital, and posterior superior temporal cortices and strong correlations extend into anterior ventral temporal, anterior superior temporal sulcal and lateral prefrontal cortices (lower image).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding from Figure 7.

claim: Approximately 35 principal components were sufficient to account for the information content of one hour of the movie, as indexed by bsMVPC.
source: Applying PCA to the model space for ventral temporal cortex, developed based on patterns of activity evoked by a naturalistic movie, revealed that approximately 35 principal components (PCs) were sufficient to account for the information content of one hour of the movie, as indexed by bsMVPC (Haxby et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a specific finding supported by citation.

claim: The face versus object category selective distinction does not emerge as one of the top dimensions but only as a mixture of PCs.
source: Comparison of the topographies for the top PCs with the topography for face versus object category selective areas (Figure 8a), shows that this functional distinction does not emerge as one of the top dimensions but only as a mixture of PCs (Figure 8a rightmost images)
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 8a.

claim: Response variance for a dynamic, naturalistic movie along the face versus object dimension comprised 7% of the total variance and 12% of the variance accounted for by the 35-dimensional model.
source: Response variance for a dynamic, naturalistic movie along that dimension comprised 7% of the total variance and 12% of the variance accounted for by the 35-dimensional model (58% of the total variance in movie response data was accounted for by all 35 dimensions, cross-validated on independent data; Figure 8b).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding supported by reference to Figure 8b.

claim: The first PC accounted for over three times more variance (22%, cross-validated) than the face versus object dimension.
source: By contrast, the first PC accounted for over three times more variance (22%, cross-validated)
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding.

claim: The mean correlation of movie time-series for the face versus object dimension and the animacy continuum dimension is 0.83.
source: The mean correlation of movie time-series for these two dimensions is 0.83
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding.

claim: The mean correlation of topographies for the face versus object dimension and the animacy continuum dimension in ventral temporal cortex is 0.77.
source: and the mean correlation of their topographies in ventral temporal cortex is 0.77.
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding.

claim: The animacy continuum dimension accounts for over 50% of variance in the responses to still images of animals and objects.
source: Although this animacy continuum dimension accounts for over 50% of variance in the responses to still images of animals and objects (Sha et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The animacy continuum dimension accounts for only 6% of variance in responses to the movie.
source: it accounts for only 6% of variance in responses to the movie.
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding.

claim: For anatomically aligned data, intersubject correlations of profiles for neighboring loci are only slightly lower than correlations of profiles for loci at the same location.
source: For anatomically aligned data, intersubject correlations of profiles for neighboring loci are only slightly lower than correlations of profiles for loci at the same location.
evidence: This describes a property of anatomically aligned data.

claim: For data projected from the common model into one subject's anatomy, the spatial point-spread function is dramatically steeper with large differences in intersubject correlation of profiles from the same location and correlations of profiles from contiguous locations.
source: For data projected from the common model into one subject's anatomy, the function is dramatically steeper with large differences in intersubject correlation of profiles from the same location and correlations of profiles from contiguous locations (Figure 9)
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 9.

claim: The common model preserves the distinctiveness of functional profiles with a spatial granularity of a single voxel or vertex (~3 mm).
source: indicating that the common model preserves the distinctiveness of functional profiles with a spatial granularity of a single voxel or vertex (~3 mm).
evidence: This is an inference from the spatial PSF analysis.

claim: This level of spatial granularity was found for all cortical fields tested in occipital, temporal, parietal, and prefrontal cortices.
source: This level of spatial granularity was found for all cortical fields tested in occipital, temporal, parietal, and prefrontal cortices.
evidence: This describes the generality of the spatial granularity finding.

claim: A within-subject PSF for connectivity profiles calculated using resting-state fMRI data from independent sessions in the same subject was equivalent to the between-subject PSF.
source: A within-subject PSF for connectivity profiles calculated using resting-state fMRI data from independent sessions in the same subject was equivalent to the between-subject PSF.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the spatial PSF analysis.

claim: Fine-grained structure in the connectome was not recognized prior to the development of a hyperaligned model of the human connectome.
source: This fine-grained structure in the connectome was not recognized prior to the development of a hyperaligned model of the human connectome.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: Even though hyperalignment makes individual differences much smaller, the residual differences are substantially more reliable across independent data samples than those based on anatomically aligned data.
source: Surprisingly, even though hyperalignment makes individual differences much smaller, as expected, the residual differences are substantially more reliable across independent data samples than those based on anatomically aligned data
evidence: This is a key finding from the individual differences analysis.

claim: The increased reliability of individual differences can be attributed to individual differences in the information encoded in fine-scale topographies.
source: and this increased reliability can be attributed to individual differences in the information encoded in fine-scale topographies (Figure 10b).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 10b.

claim: The reliabilities of individual differences based on coarse-scale topographies are effectively equivalent for anatomically-aligned and hyperaligned data.
source: The reliabilities of individual differences based on coarse-scale topographies are effectively equivalent for anatomically-aligned and hyperaligned data
evidence: This is a specific finding from the individual differences analysis.

claim: The individual differences based on residual data in fine-scale topographies are markedly more reliable for hyperaligned data than for anatomically-aligned data.
source: whereas the individual differences based on residual data in fine-scale topographies are markedly more reliable for hyperaligned data than for anatomically-aligned data.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the individual differences analysis.

claim: The individual differences in the information encoded in fine-scale topographies are more predictive of cognitive differences, such as general intelligence.
source: The individual differences in the information encoded in fine-scale topographies also are more predictive of cognitive differences, such as general intelligence (Feilong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Previous work using anatomically-aligned connectomes has investigated only individual differences in coarse scale, inter-areal connectivity.
source: Previous work using anatomically-aligned connectomes has investigated only individual differences in coarse scale, inter-areal connectivity (Braga and Buckner, 2017; Dubois et al., 2018; Finn et al., 2015; Gordon et al., 2017; Kong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The most informative individual differences in cortical function reside in fine-scale patterns.
source: but it appears that the most informative individual differences in cortical function reside in fine-scale patterns.
evidence: This is an inference from the individual differences analysis.

claim: Hyperalignment affords investigation of differences at the fine-scale level of organization and factors out confounding variability due to topographic misalignment.
source: Hyperalignment affords investigation of differences at this level of organization and factors out confounding variability due to topographic misalignment.
evidence: This describes an advantage of hyperalignment for studying individual differences.

claim: Most other approaches to modeling shared information in cortical topographies have mostly overlooked information encoded in fine-scale topographic patterns.
source: Other approaches to modeling shared information in cortical topographies have mostly overlooked information encoded in fine-scale topographic patterns.
evidence: This is a claim about the limitations of prior approaches.

claim: Most other approaches have focused on areal structure.
source: Most have focused on areal structure (Gordon et al., 2017; Langs et al., 2016; Langs et al., 2014; Yeo et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Representational similarity analysis and pattern component modeling are closely related to hyperalignment.
source: Representational similarity analysis (RSA; Kriegeskorte et al., 2008a; Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013) and pattern component modeling (Diedrichsen and Kriegeskorte, 2017) are closely related to hyperalignment.
evidence: This describes the relationship between different approaches.

claim: RSA and pattern component modeling focus on the vector geometry of response patterns in cortical areas as the common basis for representation of information that is shared across subjects.
source: These approaches focus on the vector geometry of response patterns in cortical areas as the common basis for representation of information that is shared across subjects and reveals individual differences (Charest et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the focus of RSA and pattern component modeling, supported by citation.

claim: RSA and pattern component modeling treat the topographies that embed vector geometries as unimportant.
source: These approaches treat the topographies that embed these geometries as unimportant
evidence: This describes a limitation of RSA and pattern component modeling.

claim: RSA and pattern component modeling do not offer an explicit method for modeling the idiosyncrasies in local fine-scale topographies.
source: and, consequently, do not offer an explicit method for modeling the idiosyncrasies in local fine-scale topographies or a principled approach to rearrange information in the cortical sheet to enhance the inter-subject similarity of representational geometry in a cortical field.
evidence: This describes a limitation of RSA and pattern component modeling.

claim: The forward encoding approach models each voxel's response profile independently as a weighted sum of stimulus features and captures fine spatial-scale variation.
source: The forward encoding approach models each voxel's response profile independently as a weighted sum of stimulus features and, thereby, captures fine spatial-scale variation (Kay et al., 2008; Mitchell et al., 2008; Naselaris et al., 2011; Naselaris et al., 2009; Nishimoto et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the forward encoding approach, supported by citations.

claim: Hyperalignment and related methods afford improved cross-subject voxelwise prediction of response profiles.
source: Hyperalignment and related methods afford improved cross-subject voxelwise prediction of response profiles (Bilenko and Gallant, 2016; Güçlü and van Gerven, 2017; Nastase et al., 2020; Van Uden et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Forward encoding predefines the shared information by the stimulus feature model, and its validity is dependent on the validity and strength of that feature model.
source: Forward encoding predefines the shared information by the stimulus feature model, and its validity is dependent on the validity and strength of that feature model.
evidence: This describes a limitation of forward encoding.

claim: Forward encoding does not provide any principled way to discover the structure of information that is encoded in neural responses that is not captured by the predefined feature model.
source: It does not provide any principled way to discover the structure of information that is encoded in neural responses that is not captured by the predefined feature model.
evidence: This describes a limitation of forward encoding.

claim: Forward encoding approaches do not attempt to investigate neural responses as population codes with a representational geometry.
source: These approaches also do not attempt to investigate neural responses as population codes with a representational geometry, but simply as independent voxel-wise responses to stimulus features.
evidence: This describes a limitation of forward encoding.

claim: The conceptual framework for hyperalignment is predicated on the hypothesis that information content that is shared across brains is instantiated in varied, idiosyncratic population codes.
source: The conceptual framework for hyperalignment is predicated on the hypothesis that information content that is shared across brains is instantiated in varied, idiosyncratic population codes.
evidence: This is a fundamental hypothesis of the hyperalignment framework.

claim: Hyperalignment models shared information by preserving the interrelations among pattern vectors while remixing the functional profiles of constituent dimensions.
source: Hyperalignment models shared information by preserving the interrelations among pattern vectors – vector geometry – in a common information space while remixing the functional profiles of constituent dimensions – response tuning and functional connectivity profiles – thereby reshaping the functional profiles of the units in cortical patterns.
evidence: This describes the core mechanism of hyperalignment.

claim: The functional profiles of individual units are modeled as secondary to the information content that they support as populations.
source: Thus, the functional profiles of individual units are modeled as secondary to the information content that they support as populations.
evidence: This is a key conceptual claim of the hyperalignment framework.

claim: The commonality across brains is not modeled as common functional profiles of the individual units or as a common spatial distribution of functional profiles.
source: The commonality across brains is not modeled as common functional profiles of the individual units or as a common spatial distribution of functional profiles.
evidence: This describes what hyperalignment does not model.

claim: Traditionally, neuroscientists have focused on the tuning and connectivity profiles of individual units and the information in population responses is modeled as a secondary consequence of the aggregation of those profiles.
source: Traditionally, neuroscientists have focused on the tuning and connectivity profiles of individual units – neurons or voxels – and the information in population responses is modeled as a secondary consequence of the aggregation of those profiles (e.g. Gross et al., 1972; Hubel and Wiesel, 1959; Huth et al., 2016; Huth et al., 2012; Kay et al., 2008; Kiani et al., 2007; Sheinberg and Logothetis, 2001).
evidence: This describes the traditional approach, supported by citations.

claim: The preservation of information content in vector geometry over variations in the functional profiles of individual units suggests that the unit profiles are shaped to support the geometry, not that the vector geometry is merely a reflection of unit profiles.
source: The preservation of information content in vector geometry over variations in the functional profiles of individual units, however, suggests that the unit profiles are shaped to support the geometry, not that the vector geometry is merely a reflection of unit profiles.
evidence: This is an inference from the hyperalignment results.

claim: Unit profiles clearly develop with experience and show a perplexing complexity and variety when considered in isolation.
source: Unit profiles clearly develop with experience and show a perplexing complexity and variety when considered in isolation (Çukur et al., 2013; Kiani et al., 2007; Sheinberg and Logothetis, 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Tuning functions of varying levels of coarseness support similarity of population responses and connectivity patterns and pattern vector geometries.
source: Tuning functions of varying levels of coarseness – responses to related stimuli – support similarity of population responses and connectivity patterns (Kiani et al., 2007) and, consequently, pattern vector geometries.
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Relationships reflected in similarity of responses can be due to shared perceptual features or cognitive factors such as agency and action goals.
source: Relationships reflected in similarity of responses can be due to shared perceptual features or cognitive factors such as agency (Connolly et al., 2012; Sha et al., 2015; Thorat et al., 2019) and action goals (Nastase et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The relationships reflected in representational geometry differ by cortical field.
source: The relationships reflected in representational geometry differ by cortical field (Borghesani et al., 2016; Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Guntupalli et al., 2017; Guntupalli et al., 2016; Visconti di Oleggio Castello et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Differences in representational geometry across cortical fields reflect processing or the disentangling of target information from confounds.
source: and these differences reflect processing or the disentangling of target information from confounds (DiCarlo et al., 2012; DiCarlo and Cox, 2007; Kriegeskorte and Kievit, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The topographic organization of units with particular functional profiles may arise over the course of development and with varying experience.
source: The topographic organization of units with particular functional profiles may arise over the course of development and with varying experience (Arcaro et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Functional profiles of individual units may fluctuate over time despite retaining the information encoded at the population level.
source: These functional profiles may in fact fluctuate over time despite retaining the information encoded at the population level (Gallego et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The functional profiles of individual units need not be easily-interpretable.
source: The functional profiles of individual units need not be easily-interpretable (Ponce et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Differences in vector geometry across cortical fields in a processing system are supported by different configurations of tuning profiles of individual units.
source: Differences in vector geometry across cortical fields in a processing system are supported by different configurations of tuning profiles of individual units.
evidence: This is an inference about how information processing is implemented.

claim: The composition of varied response profiles in populations is shaped to create the varied information spaces that are required in a processing system.
source: The composition of varied response profiles in populations, therefore, is shaped to create the varied information spaces that are required in a processing system, a learning process that may rest on feedback among the cortical fields in the system.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about learning mechanisms.

claim: Deep convolutional neural networks provide a computational instantiation of a learning process guided by feedback that produces varied sets of individual units that perform the same functions.
source: Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) provide a computational instantiation of a learning process guided by feedback that produces varied sets of individual units that perform the same functions.
evidence: This draws an analogy to artificial neural networks.

claim: Like cortical systems, the individual features of CNNs vary based on initialization and network architecture, but the similarity structure of feature vectors reveals commonality of layer-specific information content across these variations.
source: Like cortical systems, the individual features of CNNs vary based on initialization and network architecture, but the similarity structure of feature vectors reveals commonality of layer-specific information content across these variations (Kornblith et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The contrast between a common deep structure for information that is instantiated in variable surface structure has a parallel in language.
source: The contrast between a common deep structure for information that is instantiated in variable surface structure has a parallel in language (Chomsky, 1965; Hockett, 1958).
evidence: This draws an analogy to linguistics, supported by citations.

claim: The same meaning can be conveyed linguistically with substantial variation in wording and sentence structure, including the words and syntax of different languages.
source: The same meaning can be conveyed linguistically with substantial variation in wording and sentence structure, including the words and syntax of different languages.
evidence: This is a general property of language.

claim: The conceptual framework of hyperalignment models a property of cortical functional architecture that is a ubiquitous property of complex biological systems, namely 'degeneracy'.
source: More broadly, the conceptual framework of hyperalignment models a property of cortical functional architecture that is a ubiquitous property of complex biological systems, namely 'degeneracy' – 'the ability of elements that are structurally different to perform the same function or yield the same output' (Edelman and Gally, 2001).
evidence: This draws a connection to the concept of degeneracy in biology, supported by citation.

claim: Degeneracy is a property of systems that evolve or develop or learn and are characterized by complex interactions among constituent elements.
source: Degeneracy is a property of systems that evolve or develop or learn and are characterized by complex interactions among constituent elements.
evidence: This describes properties of degenerate systems.

claim: Unplanned interactions in degenerate systems allow unexpected new functions to emerge or to be learned.
source: Unplanned interactions in degenerate systems allow unexpected new functions to emerge or to be learned.
evidence: This describes a property of degenerate systems.

claim: Different instantiations of elements that perform the same or similar functions may be differentially adaptive to changing demands, providing a basis for evolution.
source: Different instantiations of elements that perform the same or similar functions may be differentially adaptive to changing demands, providing a basis for evolution.
evidence: This describes an evolutionary advantage of degeneracy.

claim: Degeneracy is characteristic of systems at all levels of biological organization from genetics to body movements and language.
source: Degeneracy is characteristic of systems at all levels of biological organization from genetics to body movements and language.
evidence: This describes the ubiquity of degeneracy in biology.

claim: Hyperalignment models how the variable structural elements of functional cortical architecture perform similar functions in aggregate for representation and processing of information.
source: Hyperalignment models how the variable structural elements of functional cortical architecture – local neural responses and point-to-point functional connectivities – perform similar functions in aggregate for representation and processing of information
evidence: This summarizes how hyperalignment relates to degeneracy.

claim: Hyperalignment provides a basis for studying variations in instantiations of cortical functions, which are the basis for diversity in cognitive abilities.
source: and provides a basis for studying variations in instantiations of these functions, which are the basis for diversity in cognitive abilities.
evidence: This describes an application of hyperalignment.
